The page downloads a Python WASM runtime on your first experiment. PyIceberg creates the table, Arrow writes the files, and DuckDB runs SQL locally.

Prerequisites and reading pathsStart with familiarity with tables, rows and columns. To investigate by editing code, be able to read basic SQL SELECT, WHERE and GROUP BY statements and short Python examples with function calls, lists, dictionaries and loops. This is an Iceberg course, not a first course in SQL or Python.You do not need Iceberg, Spark, Java, a cloud account or object-storage administration experience. Knowing what a Parquet file is will help; understanding its binary format is optional. The Parquet lab is a companion, not a required prerequisite.For a reading path, use the concept diagrams and worked explanations, then explain each mechanism in your own words. Optional captioned videos and transcripts cover selected processes. Experiment checks provide evidence about the code; they do not certify mastery merely for pressing Run.

How a lesson worksEach lesson asks one question. Predict the outcome, run the editable Python, inspect its output and the warehouse, then compare it with the worked result. Try the suggested variation and answer the explanation check.Use the optional prediction and reflection notes to record your reasoning. They are saved only in this browser. Hints offer a starting point before revealing what evidence to inspect. Each section ends with an unfamiliar scenario and a self-review rubric; use it to test transfer rather than recognition.Every run recreates that lesson’s fixture. It does not continue the previous run or previous lesson. Your code edits and review progress are saved in this browser when storage is available. The warehouse itself is held in worker memory and is lost on reload, stopping the runtime, or starting another experiment.Use Mark reviewed to track a reading path. It is a personal bookmark, not a certificate. Passing the original code check and the explanation question also marks the lesson reviewed. Variations may deliberately fail the original check; inspect the result and explain why.

Self-hosted runtime assets cost roughly 46 MB uncompressed on first load. Browser caching and compression affect actual transfer. Startup may take tens of seconds. Nothing is downloaded for computation until you select Run. Static lesson assets load normally.

There are no cloud credentials, remote catalog services, query servers or analytics trackers. After runtime assets load, experiments require no network services. This is not an offline-installed application; navigation after a full offline reload depends on the browser cache.

Read the evidence correctlyReal Iceberg means the operation uses PyIceberg and real table files.Model labels mean an explicit teaching calculation or policy scenario. These do not demonstrate distributed services or production enforcement.Candidate records are rows in selected files, not necessarily rows examined by every downstream operator.Selected file bytes sum file sizes; they are not measured bytes read, HTTP traffic or billing.Elapsed time includes fixture setup, the example and its check in the worker. It is not an isolated query benchmark.

The SQL helper first materializes an Iceberg scan as Arrow and then registers it with DuckDB. SQL WHERE clauses do not feed predicates back into the Iceberg scan. Use table.scan(row_filter=...) or metrics(predicate) when investigating Iceberg pruning.

Runtime boundariesThis pinned build supports real identity partition writes, schema changes, snapshot reads, tags, copy-on-write deletes and metadata-only snapshot expiration. Day and bucket partition writes need a native helper absent from this WASM build. Merge-on-read delete files and distributed compaction are not implemented here.Small-table consolidation uses a full overwrite. Snapshot expiration removes references but does not physically delete files in this implementation. Concurrent commits use a sequential interleaving against the real SQLite catalog. This cannot measure distributed catalog behavior, conflict timing or cluster throughput.Two compatibility shims adapt upstream Python scheduling to a synchronous executor and reject unavailable S3 filesystem use. They do not implement or synthesize Iceberg metadata.Governance exercises expose intended access paths and failure modes. Code running under the learner’s control cannot provide trusted authorization, tamper-resistant audit or proof of regulatory compliance.
Vocabulary to keep nearbyTermMeaning in this lab
CatalogResolves a table name and coordinates publication of its current metadata.
SnapshotA table state identified by an ID, with references to its manifest list.
Manifest listAn Avro file listing manifests and summaries for one snapshot.
ManifestAn Avro file containing data-file or delete-file entries and their metrics.
Field IDA stable identity for a column, independent of its current name or position.
Partition specificationSource fields and transforms used to partition files. Old files retain the spec that wrote them.
PruningRuling out files or other units that cannot contain matching data.
Residual predicateThe condition still needing evaluation after coarse metadata decisions.
Copy-on-writeReplacing affected data files to apply row changes.
Merge-on-readCombining data with supported row-delete information during reads.
CompactionRewriting data into a more useful physical layout while preserving its logical contents.
ExpirationRemoving eligible snapshot history from current table metadata; physical cleanup is a separate concern here.
Orphan fileA file no longer referenced by the relevant table state and retention graph. Age and in-flight writes matter before removal.
Optimistic concurrencyPreparing a change, then validating its requirements against current state at commit time.

Inspect and exportAfter a run, open the warehouse list to inspect actual JSON, Avro or Parquet metadata. Export warehouse downloads a ZIP containing the catalog and files, including retained historical data. It exports the most recent experiment in this worker. It does not persist that warehouse into the next lesson.Metadata contains absolute file:///warehouse/... paths. To reopen an export, extract at /warehouse in an isolated environment and use a compatible PyIceberg SqlCatalog with sqlite:////warehouse/catalog.db. Moving it elsewhere requires a deliberate path relocation; an arbitrary unzip location is not portable. The exported SQLite catalog is an instructional local catalog, not a REST catalog.Export evidence separately to save your code, fixture, check result and table state. No cloud upload is performed.

If something failsUse Stop / restart to terminate an experiment that is taking too long, then run again. This discards its in-memory warehouse. Reset code restores the original example. If the runtime cannot load, check access to this site’s static assets and available browser memory. Read the worked explanation while it loads; try a current desktop Chrome, Firefox or Safari.

Why start here?Suppose your sales data lives in Parquet files. A file tells you what is inside it, but a folder listing cannot reliably tell you which files form the current table. What if a writer has uploaded new files but has not finished its change? Which version should a dashboard read?Apache Iceberg is a table format: it adds metadata that describes table states and the files belonging to them. This lets readers use a complete, published table state while writers prepare changes. To understand the performance, safe updates and governance decisions later in this course, we first need to follow how a query finds that state.The first step is the catalog, which maps a table name to its current metadata location. We begin with an empty table to make one distinction visible: a table can already have a name, schema (its columns and types) and metadata before it contains any data files.

Before you start: be familiar with tables, rows and columns. Basic SQL and reading short Python examples help with the experiments. Iceberg knowledge is not assumed. You can follow the worked explanations without running code. Prerequisites and laboratory guide.

Resolve a table name to its current metadata file.Imagine a sales dashboard querying shop.orders: orders is the table, and shop groups related tables. Before opening data files, the reader asks the catalog which metadata file describes that table now.
The ideaA table name is an address, not a container of rows. The catalog’s pointer tells a reader which metadata version is current.

CatalogResolves a table name and coordinates publication of its current metadata.
SnapshotA table state identified by an ID, with references to its manifest list.
Manifest listAn Avro file listing manifests and summaries for one snapshot.
ManifestAn Avro file containing data-file or delete-file entries and their metrics.
Field IDA stable identity for a column, independent of its current name or position.
Partition specificationSource fields and transforms used to partition files. Old files retain the spec that wrote them.
PruningRuling out files or other units that cannot contain matching data.
Residual predicateThe row condition that still needs to be tested inside the files a planner has selected.
Copy-on-writeReplacing affected data files to apply row changes.
Merge-on-readCombining data with supported row-delete information during reads.
CompactionRewriting data into a more useful physical layout while preserving its logical contents.
ExpirationRemoving eligible snapshot history from current table metadata; physical cleanup is a separate concern here.
Orphan fileA file not referenced by any table state that must be retained. Cleanup must also account for writes still in progress and a safe minimum file age.
Optimistic concurrencyPreparing a change, then validating its requirements against current state at commit time.
